claim: Post-mortem magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides the opportunity to acquire high-resolution datasets to investigate neuroanatomy and validate the origins of image contrast through microscopy comparisons.
source: Post-mortem magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides the opportunity to acquire high-resolution datasets to investigate neuroanatomy and validate the origins of image contrast through microscopy comparisons.
evidence: This is a general statement about the capabilities of post-mortem MRI, drawing on established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The Digital Brain Bank is accessible at open.win.ox.ac.uk/DigitalBrainBank.
source: The Digital Brain Bank is accessible at open.win.ox.ac.uk/DigitalBrainBank.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the location of the resource.

claim: The first Digital Brain Bank data release includes 21 distinctive whole-brain diffusion MRI datasets for structural connectivity investigations.
source: The first Digital Brain Bank data release includes 21 distinctive whole-brain diffusion MRI datasets for structural connectivity investigations, alongside microscopy and complementary MRI modalities.

claim: The first release includes one of the highest-resolution whole-brain human diffusion MRI datasets ever acquired.
source: This includes one of the highest-resolution whole-brain human diffusion MRI datasets ever acquired, whole-brain diffusion MRI in fourteen nonhuman primate species, and one of the largest post-mortem whole-brain cohort imaging studies in neurodegeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dataset specifications described in the manuscript (500 μm isotropic resolution).

claim: The first release includes whole-brain diffusion MRI in fourteen nonhuman primate species.
source: This includes one of the highest-resolution whole-brain human diffusion MRI datasets ever acquired, whole-brain diffusion MRI in fourteen nonhuman primate species, and one of the largest post-mortem whole-brain cohort imaging studies in neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is supported by the data being made available and the species list provided in the manuscript.

claim: The first release includes one of the largest post-mortem whole-brain cohort imaging studies in neurodegeneration.
source: This includes one of the highest-resolution whole-brain human diffusion MRI datasets ever acquired, whole-brain diffusion MRI in fourteen nonhuman primate species, and one of the largest post-mortem whole-brain cohort imaging studies in neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is supported by the Human ALS MRI-Histology dataset containing 12 ALS and 3 control brains.

claim: MRI occupies a unique position in the neuroscience toolkit.
source: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) occupies a unique position in the neuroscience toolkit.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge about MRI's role in neuroscience.

claim: In humans, MRI is used at the single-subject level diagnostically and is increasingly deployed at the population level in epidemiology.
source: In humans, MRI is used at the single-subject level diagnostically and is increasingly deployed at the population level in epidemiology (Marcus et al., 2007; Miller et al., 2016; Snoek et al., 2021; Van Essen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MRI is well-established in the context of imaging causal manipulations in experimental organisms ranging from mice to nonhuman primates.
source: MRI is well-established in the context of imaging causal manipulations in experimental organisms ranging from mice (Denic et al., 2011; Thiessen et al., 2013) to nonhuman primates (Absinta et al., 2017; Klink et al., 2021) and provides precise measurements in cellular and tissue preparations (Wilhelm et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MRI provides precise measurements in cellular and tissue preparations.
source: MRI is well-established in the context of imaging causal manipulations in experimental organisms ranging from mice (Denic et al., 2011; Thiessen et al., 2013) to nonhuman primates (Absinta et al., 2017; Klink et al., 2021) and provides precise measurements in cellular and tissue preparations (Wilhelm et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Post-mortem MRI provides unique opportunities for common measurements across multiple species or MRI and microscopy measurements in the same brain tissue.
source: Post-mortem MRI provides unique opportunities for such common measurements.
evidence: This is based on the capabilities of post-mortem MRI as described in the manuscript and established knowledge.

claim: MRI in post-mortem tissue can be used to identify the origins of image contrast through integration with microscopy.
source: MRI in post-mortem tissue can be used to identify the origins of image contrast through integration with microscopy (Keren et al., 2015; Langkammer et al., 2012; Mollink et al., 2017), directly addressing concerns over the nonspecificity of MRI signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Post-mortem MRI data share common signal forming mechanisms with in vivo MRI and a common tissue state with microscopy.
source: In this context, post-mortem MRI data are important because they share common signal forming mechanisms with in vivo MRI and a common tissue state with microscopy, providing a framework for investigation across multiple spatial scales.
evidence: This is based on the physical principles of MRI and the nature of post-mortem tissue.

claim: Post-mortem MRI facilitates comparative anatomy investigations in species that are not traditionally accessible for in vivo imaging.
source: Post-mortem MRI facilitates comparative anatomy investigations in species that are not traditionally accessible for in vivo imaging (Berns et al., 2015; Bhagwandin et al., 2017; Grewal et al., 2020; Heuer et al., 2019), including extinct species (Berns and Ashwell, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Post-mortem MRI can be used to study extinct species.
source: Post-mortem MRI facilitates comparative anatomy investigations in species that are not traditionally accessible for in vivo imaging (Berns et al., 2015; Bhagwandin et al., 2017; Grewal et al., 2020; Heuer et al., 2019), including extinct species (Berns and Ashwell, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Long post-mortem scans provide the opportunity to push the boundaries of spatial resolution, providing whole human brain coverage reaching voxel sizes of 100–500 μm.
source: Long post-mortem scans provide the opportunity to push the boundaries of spatial resolution, providing whole human brain coverage reaching voxel sizes of 100–500 μm (Edlow et al., 2019; Foxley et al., 2016; Fritz et al., 2019; Weigel et al., 2021), edging closer to microscopy techniques but benefitting from compatibility with in vivo imaging.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Post-mortem MRI is a nondestructive technique that enables the examination of tissue microstructure whilst preserving tissue.
source: As a nondestructive technique, post-mortem MRI enables the examination of tissue microstructure whilst preserving tissue, facilitating repeat MRI measurements with novel contrasts and technologies; and more generally, its integration with tools for post-mortem investigations (e.g., histopathology or proteomics).
evidence: This is based on the fundamental properties of MRI as a technique.

Tview has been developed for efficient browsing of imaging data spanning drastically different spatial scales, from submicron resolution microscopy to millimeter MRI acquisitions.

source: This potential is most clearly seen in the Human Callosum MRI-PLI-Histology dataset, which provides diffusion MRI (400 μm isotropic), alongside complementary PLI (4 μm in-plane), and histology (myelin and astrocytes) (0.25 μm in-plane) in three excised human corpus callosum samples (Mollink et al., 2017).

claim: Post-mortem tissue that has undergone chemical preservation with aldehyde solutions is characterized by short relaxation time constants (T1, T2, and T2*) compared to in vivo tissue.

claim: The lab addressed the imaging environment of fixed, post-mortem tissue and comparatively low gradient-strengths by investing in alternative MR sequences to increase SNR.
source: Here, we addressed the imaging environment of fixed, post-mortem tissue and comparatively low gradient-strengths by investing in alternative MR sequences to increase SNR.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methodological approach taken.

claim: All brains and tissue samples in the first release of the Digital Brain Bank were chemically fixed using aldehyde solutions to prevent decomposition.
source: All brains and tissue samples in the first release of the Digital Brain Bank were chemically fixed using aldehyde solutions (e.g., formalin) to prevent decomposition (D'Arceuil and de Crespigny, 2007) and minimize deformation during the course of scanning.
evidence: This is a direct statement about sample preparation, supported by a citation.

claim: All fixed nonhuman brains and excised tissue blocks scanned at the University of Oxford were prepared by soaking the samples in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) prior to scanning.
source: All fixed nonhuman brains and excised tissue blocks scanned at the University of Oxford were prepared by soaking the samples in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) prior to scanning, which increases image SNR by raising T2-values closer to those found in vivo (Shepherd et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a direct statement about sample preparation, supported by a citation.

claim: Soaking samples in PBS increases image SNR by raising T2-values closer to those found in vivo.
source: All fixed nonhuman brains and excised tissue blocks scanned at the University of Oxford were prepared by soaking the samples in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) prior to scanning, which increases image SNR by raising T2-values closer to those found in vivo (Shepherd et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: PBS soaking was not performed in whole human brains because brain size necessitates a soaking time of multiple weeks for the buffer fluid to penetrate throughout tissue.
source: This was not performed in whole human brains, as brain size necessitates a soaking time of multiple weeks for the buffer fluid to penetrate throughout tissue (Dawe et al., 2009; Tendler et al., 2021; Yong-Hing et al., 2005) which was incompatible with our experimental design.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental approach, supported by citations.

claim: Soaking tissue for an insufficient time can lead to artificial 'boundaries' in resulting images, where PBS has not penetrated into deep tissue.
source: We note that soaking tissue for an insufficient time can lead to artificial 'boundaries' in resulting images, where PBS has not penetrated into deep tissue (Miller et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: All samples scanned at the University of Oxford were imaged in a proton-free susceptibility-matched fluid (Fomblin LC08 or Fluorinert FC-3283).
source: All samples scanned at the University of Oxford were imaged in a proton-free susceptibility-matched fluid (Fomblin LC08, Solvay Solexis; or Fluorinert FC-3283, 3M).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental setup.

claim: The choice of a proton-free fluid means that there is no signal outside of the brain, minimizing the required field-of-view for any acquisitions.
source: The choice of a proton-free fluid means that there is no signal outside of the brain, bringing the additional advantage of minimizing the required field-of-view for any acquisitions, and addressing scaling issues arising from a bright background signal.
evidence: This is based on the properties of proton-free fluids in MRI.

claim: A two-stage custom holder was built for whole human brain imaging.
source: For whole human brain imaging, we built a two-stage custom holder (Appendix 3—figure 1), which has become the standard for all of our whole-brain human imaging experiments.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental setup.

claim: The custom holder was designed to fit into a 32-channel receive/1-channel transmit head coil.
source: The holder was designed to fit into a 32-channel receive/1-channel transmit head coil (Nova Medical), securing brains throughout the acquisition, and contains a spherical cavity to minimize field-inhomogeneities across the brain.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the design of the holder.

claim: The custom holder contains a spherical cavity to minimize field-inhomogeneities across the brain.
source: The holder was designed to fit into a 32-channel receive/1-channel transmit head coil (Nova Medical), securing brains throughout the acquisition, and contains a spherical cavity to minimize field-inhomogeneities across the brain.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the design of the holder.

claim: The custom holder enables brains to be placed in a consistent position equivalent to an in vivo supine scan.
source: The holder enables brains to be placed in a consistent position (equivalent to an in vivo supine scan), minimizing variability of B0-orientation dependent effects (e.g., susceptibility anisotropy; Liu, 2010), as well as avoiding any potential motion.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the design of the holder, with a citation for the B0-orientation effects.

claim: The convergence of T1 relaxation times for gray and white matter in formalin-fixed post-mortem tissue leads to poor contrast with conventional T1-weighted structural protocols.
source: However, the convergence of T1 relaxation times for gray and white matter in formalin-fixed post-mortem tissue leads poor contrast with conventional T1-weighted structural protocols (Miller et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: All structural MRIs available in the first data release were acquired using either a balanced SSFP (bSSFP) or T2-weighted sequence.
source: All structural MRIs available in the first data release were acquired using either a balanced SSFP (bSSFP) or T2-weighted sequence, which demonstrate excellent gray/white matter contrast in fixed post-mortem tissue.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the acquisition methods used.

claim: bSSFP and T2-weighted sequences demonstrate excellent gray/white matter contrast in fixed post-mortem tissue.
source: All structural MRIs available in the first data release were acquired using either a balanced SSFP (bSSFP) or T2-weighted sequence, which demonstrate excellent gray/white matter contrast in fixed post-mortem tissue.
evidence: This is based on the known properties of these sequences in post-mortem tissue.

claim: bSSFP signal forming mechanisms lead to an extremely high SNR-efficiency, affording the acquisition of ultra-high resolution (<500 μm) imaging volumes.
source: Notably, bSSFP signal forming mechanisms lead to an extremely high SNR-efficiency (even when considering the reduced T1 and T2 of post-mortem tissue), affording the acquisition of ultra-high resolution (<500 μm) imaging volumes to delineate fine tissue structures in large post-mortem samples.
evidence: This is based on the known properties of bSSFP sequences.

claim: Contrast in bSSFP and T2-weighted structural MRI datasets is reversed in comparison to conventional in vivo T1-weighted acquisitions.
source: Contrast in bSSFP and T2-weighted structural MRI datasets is reversed in comparison to conventional in vivo T1-weighted acquisitions (i.e., gray matter appears bright, and white matter appears dark).
evidence: This is based on the known contrast mechanisms of these sequences.

claim: Post-mortem diffusion MRI is particularly challenging due to the MR-relevant properties of fixed tissue.
source: Post-mortem diffusion MRI is particularly challenging due to the MR-relevant properties of fixed tissue, with reductions in measured relaxation time constants T1, T2, and T2* (Birkl et al., 2016; Birkl et al., 2018; Dawe et al., 2009; Kamman et al., 1985; Nagara et al., 1987; Pfefferbaum et al., 2004; Shepherd et al., 2009; Thelwall et al., 2006), and diffusivity (D'Arceuil et al., 2007; Shepherd et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2003; Sun et al., 2005; Thelwall et al., 2006) routinely reported in literature.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: To achieve high SNR in post-mortem diffusion MRI, specialized preclinical systems and tissue preparation methods are often required.
source: To achieve high SNR in these conditions, specialized preclinical systems and tissue preparation methods are often required (Roebroeck et al., 2019), with many groups focusing on tissue sections that can be scanned on rodent scanners with specialized hardware (Beaujoin et al., 2018; Calabrese et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The lab has invested considerably into the use of diffusion-weighted steady-state free precession (DW-SSFP) to achieve high-SNR datasets in large post-mortem samples.
source: Over the past decade, our lab has invested considerably into the use of an alternative diffusion imaging technique, diffusion-weighted steady-state free precession (DW-SSFP) (Kaiser et al., 1974; Le Bihan, 1988; Merboldt et al., 1989a; Merboldt et al., 1989b), to achieve high-SNR datasets in large post-mortem samples.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methodological approach, supported by citations.

claim: DW-SSFP is well suited to the environment of fixed post-mortem tissue, achieving strong diffusion weighting and rapid signal sampling, even when hardware achieves limited gradient amplitudes and when T2 values are low.
source: DW-SSFP is well suited to the environment of fixed post-mortem tissue, achieving strong diffusion weighting and rapid signal sampling, even when hardware achieves limited gradient amplitudes and when T2 values are low (McNab et al., 2009; Vasung et al., 2019; Wilkinson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The DW-SSFP sequence has demonstrated improved SNR-efficiency compared to conventional DW-SE when imaging post-mortem tissue.
source: The DW-SSFP sequence has demonstrated improved SNR-efficiency compared to conventional DW-SE when imaging post-mortem tissue (Miller et al., 2012), further enhanced at ultra-high field (7T) (Foxley et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Small brains and excised tissue blocks imaged on preclinical systems were scanned using conventional DW-SE sequences.
source: Small brains and excised tissue blocks imaged on preclinical systems were scanned using conventional DW-SE sequences, where tissue preparation and powerful diffusion gradients provide imaging volumes with high SNR.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental approach used.

claim: Diffusion imaging for larger post-mortem samples scanned on a human scanner was performed using DW-SSFP.
source: Diffusion imaging for larger post-mortem samples scanned on a human scanner (Siemens 7T Magnetom) was performed using DW-SSFP.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental approach used.

claim: The majority of diffusion datasets from the Digital Brain Bank provide derived diffusivity estimates in the form of diffusion tensor and/or ball and sticks model parameters.
source: To facilitate cross-dataset comparisons, the majority of diffusion datasets from the Digital Brain Bank provide derived diffusivity estimates in the form of diffusion tensor and/or ball and sticks model parameters (Behrens et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data provided, supported by a citation.

claim: The DW-SSFP signal does not have a well-defined b-value.
source: Importantly, the DW-SSFP signal does not have a well-defined b-value (McNab and Miller, 2010; Tendler et al., 2020a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: For all DW-SSFP datasets acquired in whole human brains, a recently proposed approach was utilized to transform DW-SSFP datasets acquired at two flip angles into equivalent measurements at a single, well-defined b-value.
source: For all DW-SSFP datasets acquired in whole human brains (e.g., the Human ALS MRI-Histology dataset and the Human High-Resolution Diffusion MRI-PLI dataset), we utilized a recently proposed approach to transform DW-SSFP datasets acquired at two flip angles into equivalent measurements at a single, well-defined b-value (Tendler et al., 2020a; Tendler et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the processing approach, supported by citations.

claim: The approach to transform DW-SSFP datasets facilitates within dataset comparisons, alongside comparisons with datasets acquired with the DW-SE sequence.
source: This facilitates within dataset comparisons, alongside comparisons with datasets acquired with the DW-SE sequence.
evidence: This is based on the properties of the transformation approach.

claim: The transformation approach was not possible for the nonhuman DW-SSFP datasets due to differences in the acquisition protocol.
source: However, this approach was not possible for the nonhuman DW-SSFP datasets due to differences in the acquisition protocol.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the limitations of the processing approach.

claim: The nonhuman DW-SSFP datasets are recommended to be primarily used for structural connectivity (e.g., tractography) investigations.
source: Conservatively, we recommend the nonhuman DW-SSFP datasets to be primarily used for structural connectivity (e.g., tractography) investigations.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the properties of the data.

claim: Differences in the number of diffusion directions, choice of b-value, imaging resolution, and SNR exist across datasets.
source: More generally, differences in the number of diffusion directions, choice of b-value (for DW-SE and DW-SSFP transformed datasets), imaging resolution, and SNR exist across datasets, a result of available scanning hardware, scanning time, experimental design, and sample properties (e.g., type of fixative used and size of the brain).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the variability in the datasets.

claim: These limitations can lead to differences in resulting diffusivity estimates and should be considered when performing comparisons across different datasets in the Digital Brain Bank.
source: These limitations can lead to differences in resulting diffusivity estimates and should be considered when performing comparisons across different datasets in the Digital Brain Bank.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement based on the known effects of acquisition parameters on diffusivity estimates.

source: Quantitative T1 and T2 maps are provided with the post-mortem whole-brain human datasets, acquired using conventional turbo inversion-recovery (TIR) and turbo spin-echo (TSE) sequences.

source: Notably, T1-convergence of gray and white matter in fixed post-mortem tissue leads to low contrast on T1 maps, as described in the Structural MRI section above.

source: T1 maps were fitted assuming mono-exponential signal recovery.

source: Whole human brain quantitative T2* and quantitative susceptibility maps are available in a subset of brains provided with the Human ALS MRI-Histology dataset.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data provided.

evidence: This is a direct statement about the acquisition and processing methods, supported by a citation.

claim: Post-mortem imaging experiments combining MRI and microscopy are routinely used to validate the origins of image contrast.
